units: the yard gate is opened at sunrise by the caretaker
the yard floor is swept in front of the letter boxes
the plant tubs under the porch are watered after the sweeping
parcels are piled against a wall in the middle of the day
the children of the building use the yard as a play area in the afternoon
the children's racket is tolerated until dusk
a single lamp with damaged glass lights the way to the staircase
the gate is locked again and the fire exit checked before nightfall
this arrangement has never been set down in any written rules
text: The first light reaches the inner yard before anyone else does. The caretaker unlocks the gate, whose cracked latch still puts up a fight against the key, then sweeps the gritty paving stones in front of the letter boxes. The two plant tubs beneath the porch are watered once the sweeping is done. Around midday the delivery men stack their parcels against the far wall, and the passage narrows to a cluttered corridor. By afternoon the children of the building are rolling their balls across it, and the caretaker puts up with the racket until dusk. The windows light up one by one and quiet settles again. A single lamp, its glass chipped, marks the way to the staircase. Before nightfall the gate is locked once more and the fire exit checked. Nothing in this steady round has ever been set down in writing.

units: mending an appliance now costs more than buying another one
the high price of spare parts puts people off calling a repairer
appliances in working order are thrown into the recycling bins
the build-up of discards pushes up the bill for treating waste
this expense is carried by the community
the cheapest choice for one person brings the highest cost for everyone
bringing the price of parts down would be part of the remedy
making instruction manuals available is the second measure proposed
text: Mending a broken appliance now costs more than buying another one, and that reversal has quietly reshaped our everyday habits. Spare parts sell at such a price that nobody calls a repairer when a lid cracks or a handle works itself loose. The result is plain to see in the recycling bins, where machines barely used at all sit beside wobbly chairs that a screwdriver would have saved. All those discards push up the bill for treating waste, and the bill lands squarely on the community. So the loop closes: the cheapest choice for one household turns into the heaviest outlay for everybody. Breaking it would mean bringing the price of parts down and putting instruction manuals within reach of anyone who asks for them. Until that happens, the repair workshop will remain something of a curiosity.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a neighbour mends the other tenants' clothes for nothing
she has sewn since she was a teenager without any training
her sewing machine came from her mother
the table holding the machine is unsteady and propped up with cardboard
the ceiling light was too weak to tell a dark thread from dark cloth
the poor light made her seams go wrong
a tenant from downstairs found her an adjustable lamp at a second-hand market
the lamp gathers the beam where it is needed
she refuses payment and asks for a hot drink instead
text: You know the sort of neighbour I mean: the one who takes in everyone's torn clothes and hands them back mended, and never asks for anything. She has sewn since she was a teenager, without a single day of training. Her machine came down from her mother, and it stood on a wobbly table that she propped up with a folded scrap of cardboard. The trouble was the light. That dim ceiling bulb never let her pick out a dark thread against dark cloth, so her seams wandered, she lost her temper, she began again. A tenant from downstairs turned up with an adjustable lamp from a second-hand market, its shiny reflector gathering the beam exactly where she needed it. Now she takes up a frayed hem in a couple of stitches and will not hear of being paid. She asks for a hot drink, sits down, tells workshop stories, and the whole corridor gains by it.

units: two food shops face each other at the entrance to the neighbourhood
the first fills a narrow, poorly heated room
fruit in the first shop is weighed by hand
the owner of the first shop calls out his prices aloud
the second has a far wider range and clear labels
the second offers a till with no member of staff
the fruit from the narrow shop has a frank scent
the fruit from the shop opposite is even in size but tasteless
the shopper decides by mood and hardly ever by reason
text: Two food shops face each other at the entrance to the neighbourhood, and the contrast repays a moment of close attention. The first fills a cramped, poorly heated room where crates are stacked as high as the ceiling; the fruit is weighed out by hand and the owner calls out his prices aloud. The second, all gleaming windows, carries a far wider range, labels everything clearly and offers a till with nobody standing behind it. In use, the gap in quality does not follow the gap in comfort. Tomatoes from the cramped room ripen where they lie and keep a frank scent; those from the shop opposite are firm, even in size and utterly without taste. On one side you pay for discomfort and flavour, on the other for ease and blandness. In the end shoppers decide by mood, and hardly ever by reason.

units: the writer of the letter writes from the table where meals were taken together
the floor by the window is cracked and has not been replaced
the rug in the hall has lost its fringes
the teapot chipped at the spout is still used every evening
one arm of the armchair is worn through to the threads
a shawl left behind by the reader lies on that armchair
the drawer holds keys, postcards and a worn-down pencil
the plants on the ledge survive despite careless watering
the door creaks and still shuts badly
text: I am writing from the kitchen, at the table where we used to eat together. Nothing has changed, and that is what I wanted to tell you. The floor by the window is still cracked; I gave up on replacing it, it belongs to the room now. The rug in the hall has lost its fringes and I step over it without thinking. That teapot you hated, chipped at the spout, does its work every evening. One arm of the armchair has worn through to the threads, and the shawl you left behind lies folded across it. In the drawer there are your keys, a stack of postcards and a pencil worn down to nothing. Out on the ledge the plants hold on, though I water them carelessly. I tidy very little, as you know. Yet I am attached to these battered things the way one is attached to familiar handwriting. Come back whenever you like: the door creaks, and it shuts no better than before.

units: a dark ring low down on a partition wall signals damp coming through
what to do depends on how far things have gone
at the first stage the plaster darkens but stays dry to the touch
airing the room and pulling away the furniture that blocks the air is enough at this stage
a cheap measuring device confirms the trend
the covering turns spongy and gives way under pressure as the damp advances
the wall must then be sounded and a seal or a pipe checked
at the advanced stage the plaster comes away in patches
painting over it hides the sign without removing the cause
text: What should you do when a dark ring appears low down on a partition wall? The answer depends on how far the damp has got. Early on, the plaster darkens without lifting and the surface still feels dry under the fingers; airing the room and pulling away the furniture that blocks the air will usually do. A cheap meter confirms the trend in a couple of readings. Later, as the damp advances, the covering turns spongy and gives way under light pressure: now you sound the wall, trace the source, and check the seal of a joint or a pipe. At the advanced stage the plaster comes off in patches and leaves a gritty face; surface treatment is no longer enough, and the cause must go before anything is made good. And painting over it? That hides the sign, leaves the fault alone, and the stain comes back.

units: a tenant reports to the managing agent a dripping tap dating from the autumn
the agent cites the absence of a written request
the tenant states that he telephoned three times without an answer
the agent admits that the switchboard was overwhelmed and the messages went astray
with no report on record no tradesman was sent out
the leak therefore ran on and stained the ceiling of the flat below
the tiling under the sink has split
the repair will cost more than a washer changed at the start
the two agree that every call will be confirmed in writing the same evening
text: The tenant told the managing agent that the tap in the washroom had been dripping since the autumn. The agent replied that no written request had ever reached him, and that nothing could be set in motion without one. The tenant pointed out that he had telephoned three times and had never once been called back. The agent conceded that the switchboard had been overwhelmed and that those messages had gone astray. With no report on record, he added, no tradesman had been sent out, so the leak had run on. The tenant observed that the ceiling of the flat below now carried a stain, and that the tiling under the sink had split. The agent accepted that the repair would cost more than a washer changed back in the autumn. The two of them settled on a rule: every call would be confirmed in writing the same evening.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water every household had to draw its water outside
this chore fell mainly to children and servants
the buckets were carried up worn and slippery steps
the water stood in badly washed vessels
disease was passed on through this stored water
local authorities first opened more places to draw from
this measure shortened the walk without making things any cleaner
piping under pressure together with treatment solved the problem
putting a tap in the kitchen did away with the household store
text: Before running water ever reached the inside of people's homes, every household sent someone out to draw it from a well or from the fountain in the street. The chore fell mainly to children and to servants, who hauled heavy buckets up worn steps that were more often than not slippery. The trouble did not lie in the tiredness alone. Water stood for days on end in badly washed vessels with a slimy bottom, and disease travelled through it. Local authorities began by opening more places to draw from, a measure which shortened the walk without making the stored water any cleaner. The lasting answer came from piping under pressure, together with a treatment of the water before it was sent out. Once a tap stood in the kitchen itself, the household store vanished, and with it the chief source of contamination.

units: bread and a biscuit left out in the air overnight change in opposite directions
the bread goes hard while the biscuit goes soft
the cause shared by both changes is water on the move
fresh bread holds a great deal of water, above all in its crumb
the water in the bread drifts off into the surrounding air and the starch rearranges itself
the biscuit leaves the oven with almost no water
the biscuit takes moisture from the air and loses its snap
a wet cloth laid over the basket keeps the crumb supple
shutting the two foods away produces two opposite effects
text: Leave a slice of bread and a dry biscuit out on the table overnight, then look at them in the morning. The bread has gone hard and the biscuit has gone soft: two opposite outcomes from one single cause, which is water on the move. Fresh bread holds a great deal of it, mostly in the crumb; that water drifts off into the air, the starch rearranges itself, and the crumb turns dry and brittle. The biscuit leaves the oven with almost none, so it takes moisture from the air, its sugars grow damp, and the snap gives way to a soft, almost spongy bite. Each of them is hunting for a balance with what surrounds it. A wet cloth laid over the bread basket keeps the crumb supple. There is the trick: shut the bread away to hold its water in, shut the biscuit away to keep water out. One tin does two opposite jobs.

units: a bunch of keys was left behind on a low wall by a bus stop
a student photographed it and then handed it in at the kiosk nearby
the kiosk keeper took stock of the items attached to the bunch
the bunch carried a letter-box key and a trolley token
a building pass with nothing written on it hung there as well
the photograph stayed taped to the kiosk window for two evenings
the neighbourhood put forward several theories about who the owner was
the porter of a block recognised the model of pass and worked out the floor
the owner had not yet noticed that her keys were gone
text: It began with a bunch of keys that someone had left behind on the low wall beside a bus stop. A student photographed them, and then handed them in at the kiosk nearby. The keeper took careful stock of what lay in front of him: a letter-box key, a dull trolley token, a worn leather fob and a building pass with nothing written on it at all. The photograph stayed taped to the kiosk window for two evenings running. Then came the theories of the neighbourhood: a nurse from the block opposite, a delivery driver hurrying to finish his round, a pensioner who walks his dog on that same corner. The pass settled the matter. The porter of that block recognised the model of pass and worked out the floor. The owner, who was told late in the afternoon, had not yet noticed that her keys were gone.
